opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the most basic reason is that the human brain is an existence proof. We know these capabilities can be implemented in a physical system, and a fairly modest one: about 20 watts, a few pounds of tissue, built by an evolutionary process that wasn't optimizing for things like doing science or running a company. So there's no deep barrier saying a machine can't do what the brain does. The open question is how hard it is to find the right algorithms and how much compute you need.

On the compute side, my rough estimate is that the brain does maybe 10^15 operations per second, give or take a couple of orders of magnitude. Training runs today have already used more compute than a human brain uses over a lifetime of learning. So raw computation probably isn't what's holding us back. What we're missing is closer to software: the brain is very sample-efficient, it learns continually, it has long-horizon agency, and it integrates perception and action in ways current models don't.

Why do I expect us to close those gaps? Partly the historical track record. Algorithmic efficiency in many domains has improved by roughly an order of magnitude every couple of years, and capabilities people once considered uniquely human, like fluent language, broad knowledge, and fairly good reasoning, have fallen one after another. Partly it's the economic incentives. The capabilities current models lack, like reliably carrying out a long project, adapting on the job, or operating in messy real-world environments, are exactly what you'd need to automate most of the economy. The payoff there is tens of trillions of dollars a year, so there's enormous pressure to scale up compute and experimentation, and that experimentation is how you find better algorithms.

I'd add one caveat. This doesn't mean it happens overnight. There's a version of Moravec's paradox at play: the things that feel easy to us, like perception, motor control, and common-sense planning over long horizons, may be the hardest to get right, because evolution spent hundreds of millions of years refining them. So I expect these capabilities to arrive, but probably over a period of years to decades rather than in one sudden leap. In my view the question isn't really whether but when, and which capabilities come last.

r001.rationale: The response says economic incentives create pressure to scale up compute and experimentation, which helps find better algorithms.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, the basic reason is that I don't think there's anything magical about the brain. The brain is a physical system, it was produced by evolution, and it runs on roughly 20 watts, so there's a very concrete existence proof that you can get general intelligence out of a fairly modest compute budget. Current models are clearly missing some things the brain has: long-horizon agency, continual learning from a small number of experiences, the ability to work on a problem for months and build up context without forgetting it. But when I look at those gaps, none of them look like they require some fundamentally new principle that we have no idea how to approach. They look more like engineering and research problems that haven't been solved yet, partly because the field only recently started caring about them.

The other part of the argument is the trend. If you look back at the history of the field, people have repeatedly pointed to capabilities that models lacked and said this is the thing that's hard, this is the thing that requires real understanding. Then a few years later, with more compute and some algorithmic improvements, the models have it. The specific list of missing capabilities keeps shrinking. So my prior is that the remaining items on the list are more of the same, rather than being the one category where the pattern suddenly stops. I could be wrong about that, and I'd put real uncertainty on the timelines, especially for things like continual learning, which might need a somewhat different training setup than what we have now. But I'd be surprised if the brain turned out to have a capability that's simply unreachable for artificial systems, given that the brain itself is evidence that it's reachable.

r001.rationale: The response mentions more compute as contributing to model progress, but it does not identify running more software research experiments as a benefit of increasing compute.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think there’s a fundamental reason those capabilities should be inaccessible to AI. The human brain is a physical system, and it acquired its capabilities through an optimization process—evolution—combined with learning during a person’s lifetime. So we have an existence proof that these capabilities are possible.

That doesn’t mean scaling up current language models will necessarily reproduce everything humans can do. Some capabilities might require different architectures, different training objectives, or more interaction with the world. But I’d distinguish between saying that current methods are missing something and saying that the missing thing will be very difficult to discover. The first doesn’t establish the second.

My expectation is that, as we put more resources into AI research, we’ll find ways to close those gaps. I’m less confident about the particular route or timing than I am about the general claim that human cognitive abilities aren’t a ceiling that artificial systems fundamentally can’t reach.

r001.rationale: The response says that more resources for AI research may help close capability gaps, but it does not identify the ability to run more software research experiments as a benefit of increasing compute.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the basic reason is that the human brain is an existence proof that these capabilities can be implemented by a physical system. We don’t know how to reproduce all of them yet, but we also don’t have a strong reason to think there’s some fundamental barrier preventing us from doing so.

That doesn’t mean scaling up current models will automatically give us everything humans can do. We might need different architectures, different training methods, or systems that interact with the world and learn from that interaction. But there are strong incentives to figure those things out. If a capability is useful and humans demonstrate that it’s possible, I would generally expect research to make progress on it.

So I’m more confident about the eventual destination than about the particular route. The claim isn’t that today’s models already contain every ingredient we need. It’s that the gaps we see look more like research problems than permanent limitations of artificial intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response discusses research progress and possible architectures, but does not identify increased compute enabling more software research experiments as a benefit.
